evidence: src/domain/value-objects/DueDate.ts: `private constructor(private readonly date: Date)` plus `static fromIso(value: string): DueDate`, which throws `ValidationError` when ISO_DATE_PATTERN or Date.parse rejects the value

src/domain/value-objects/TaskStatus.ts: `private constructor(readonly value: TaskStatusValue)` plus `static from(value: string): TaskStatus`, which throws `ValidationError` and builds its message from TASK_STATUS_VALUES
Both files import only `ValidationError` from '../errors/DomainErrors', so they report bad input the same way

TaskStatus.ts: the allowed statuses are written in `TASK_STATUS_VALUES`, in the static constants TODO, IN_PROGRESS and DONE, and in the switch inside `from`. All of this is in one file, and the constructor's `TaskStatusValue` type ties the constants to the list
The two files don't depend on each other, and each date or status rule appears only once in the module
parsedVerdict.reasoning: Both files are domain value objects and share one concern: immutable, validated values used by Task. They follow the same pattern: a private constructor, a static factory that checks raw input (DueDate.fromIso, TaskStatus.from), and a domain ValidationError from ../errors/DomainErrors when the input is bad. Each file owns its own rule. The ISO date check lives only in DueDate.ts (ISO_DATE_PATTERN). The allowed statuses live only in TaskStatus.ts (TASK_STATUS_VALUES and TaskStatusValue). Neither file repeats the other's rule or works around the shared error type. Two small things are worth tidying but don't fail the rubric. First, TaskStatus.from lists the status strings again in a switch instead of using TASK_STATUS_VALUES, and isDone() compares against the string 'done' instead of TaskStatus.DONE. Both stay inside the same file, so the rule still lives in one place. Second, DueDate has no equals(), while TaskStatus does.
